newsitem.title: TOGO: France and U.S. press for Zaire talks at OAU parley.
newsitem.headline: France and U.S. press for Zaire talks at OAU parley.

text.p: France and the United States lobbied for direct talks between Zaire's warring parties on the eve of Wednesday's Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit in Togo, expressing the hope the meeting would help start the dialogue.

The joint diplomatic initiative, launched to coincide with a meeting of OAU foreign ministers on Tuesday, included a call for a truce and a warning that without talks the conflict threatened to spread in the volatile Great Lakes region.

The United States, according to a briefing document, urged ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, whose authority has crumbled in the face of relentless rebel advances, to name an individual or group to negotiate on his behalf and publicly support them.
"The Lome meeting offers a chance to concretise efforts to date and perhaps make new progress in launching negotiations," the document said.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila has sent a delegation to the summit. A delegation from Kinshasa will represent Mobutu, parliament and the caretaker government.

The Franco-American initiative, significant in that each has been accused of backing rival sides, called for all-party talks among Zaireans and an agreed electoral process to give the chaotic former Belgian colony "stable, legitimate and recognised institutions".
Kabila's rebels, who hold about a quarter of Zaire, will be attending their first major international forum.
"Kabila needs legitimacy," one Western diplomat said. "Even if they do not have direct contact it could be a start."
Some critics of the summit dismiss it as a ploy by French- speaking Africa to rescue Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 and has dominated the country since.
Togo's Pierre Koffi Panou told fellow foreign ministers the meeting was a test of the OAU's credibility and efficacity.
"The tragedy in Zaire is an illustration of a new form of conflict which, following the Cold War, threatens our whole continent," he told fellow foreign ministers on Tuesday.
France, the United States and Belgium have sent troops to Congo to evacuate their nationals from neighbouring Zaire if the need arises.
Kabila, whose forces have the upper-hand on the battlefield, has called for talks on Mobutu's departure as a condition for any truce.
Mobutu, in a statement before he returned home on Friday after fresh cancer treatment in Europe, called for a truce first.
But the revolt, which erupted in October while Mobutu was in Europe recovering from prostate cancer surgery, has drastically changed the balance of power.
Mobutu's army has collapsed in the face of determined rebel thrusts on a variety of fronts.
Many ordinary Zaireans say they are eager for change after three decades of poverty under Mobutu's rule.
From the poor quarters of the teeming capital Kinshasa to autonomy-hungry Lubumbashi in the southern mining province of Shaba, they openly welcome the prospect of the rebels' arrival.
